strengths: Addresses a relevant question: when multimodal contrastive learning recovers latent information, allowing distinct coupled variables and modality-specific nuisance factors.
Includes synthetic sensitivity studies with three-run uncertainty estimates and broad empirical coverage across four CLIP backbones, 11 few-shot datasets, and ImageNet distribution shifts.

The simple postprocessing shows promising reported gains. For ViT-B/16, PCA plus FastICA improves two-shot ImageNet accuracy from 44.97% to 46.57% and average target-domain accuracy from 32.51% to 37.13%.
weaknesses: The central proofs rely on an incorrect lemma. Lemma 5.1 in Appendix D.1 claims that the optimal normalized population loss is zero. Under the stated vMF model with matched temperature, latent-preserving embeddings instead attain -2I(zx;zt), which is negative for dependent latents. Moreover, the lemma requires paired embeddings to be equal almost surely. Because the finite-concentration vMF conditional has full support, this equality forces constant representations, contradicting the simultaneous uniformity requirement. Thus the encoder equality and nuisance removal underlying Theorems 4.1 and 4.3 are not established.

The convex-body analysis contains additional substantive errors. Equation (43) treats p(zt) as exactly uniform, although Lemma 4.2 only establishes a limiting statement as lambda approaches zero. A normalized Laplace kernel on a bounded interval generally produces a nonuniform marginal at finite lambda. Furthermore, Corollary 4.4 omits the non-Euclidean norm restriction used in Appendix E.2; Euclidean distances permit rotational ambiguity, so permutation recovery does not follow under the stated general assumptions.

The ICA justification in Section 5 conflicts with the hypersphere assumptions. Coordinates of a uniformly distributed sphere vector are dependent, and rotational symmetry provides no distinguished independent Cartesian axes for FastICA to recover. The observation about having at most M-1 independent variables does not resolve this incompatibility. The proposed local-isometry and PCA argument also supplies no formal guarantee connecting the convex-body theorem to normalized CLIP features.

The downstream experiments do not isolate disentanglement from dimensionality reduction and whitening. Appendix K changes representation dimensions substantially, yet provides no matched PCA-only or whitening-only controls. An orthogonal rotation of whitened features preserves cosine similarities and the solutions of isotropically L2-regularized linear probes. Consequently, the reported improvements cannot establish that recovering independent components supplies the benefit.

The empirical evidence does not validate identifiability as repeatedly claimed. Appendix K regresses learned representations on true latents; a rank-deficient linear projection can achieve perfect R-squared without allowing latent recovery. Reverse prediction and rank checks are needed. CelebA evidence consists of selected decoder traversals and counts of named attributes, without quantitative disentanglement measurements or matched controls; even the displayed 'Gender w/ Mustache' direction combines attributes.

The causal contribution is insufficiently formalized. The undirected edge specifies statistical dependence without intervention semantics or a characterized causal equivalence class. The manuscript does not establish what causal knowledge is recovered beyond coupled latent-variable modeling. Its strong novelty claims also exceed the demonstrated advance over the explicitly reused results of Zimmermann et al. [67].

Reproducibility and reporting remain incomplete: synthetic sample counts and optimization settings, the exact data used to fit PCA/ICA, component-selection procedures, and uncertainty across real-data runs are insufficiently specified. There is also a concrete numerical inconsistency: Figure 4 reports the RN101 baseline target average as 20.03%, although its four listed accuracies average approximately 22.03%.
